item.title: Things I Learned in 2025
item.description:
With 2025 behind us, the numbers look bleak. My five-year average for “Things I Learned” is 61 factoids, but last year fewer than 20 items made it onto the list. Not to worry, though: 2026 is on track to return to the greatness of yore.

  1. The white stuff in your cheese isn’t mold (and it isn’t “salt crystals”) 🧀 Different cheeses form different crystals. Aged cheddar and Gouda often develop calcium lactate crystals on the surface as calcium salts migrate and recrystallize. Washed-rind cheeses may show salt crystals from surface treatments. Long-aged hard cheeses such as Parmigiano-Reggiano and Grana Padano (and also aged Gouda) can develop tyrosine crystals within the paste. Tyrosine is an amino acid released during proteolysis as casein breaks down during aging, and its low solubility makes it prone to crystallize.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2024
item.description:
1. Bronze Age iron artifacts likely originated from meteorites, not from smelting terrestrial iron 🏆☄️. A geochemical approach using Fe:Co:Ni ratios can distinguish terrestrial from extraterrestrial iron. Modern iron and iron ores have distinct Fe:Co:Ni ratios compared to those found in Bronze Age artifacts.

  2. The U.S. never adopted the metric system due to Caribbean pirates 📐🏴‍☠️. When the U.S. was considering standardizing measurements, Thomas Jefferson arranged for French scientist Joseph Dombey to deliver a kilogram standard. British privateers intercepted Dombey in the Caribbean, leading to his capture and eventual death. The kilogram standard reached the U.S. too late to influence the metric system’s adoption.

item.title: Books I Read in 2023
item.description: Continuing from Books I Read in 2022, I want to provide a brief overview of the books I read in 2023. Last year, I spent a significant amount of time commuting and traveling for business, affording me ample opportunity to dive into books. As an agonizingly slow reader, my go-to choice for the past two years has been audiobooks. I anticipate a less hectic 2024, so I’m not setting a goal to read as many books this year.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2023
item.description:
More than two months into the new year, but better late than never, here is Things I Learned in 2023. This marks the fourth installment of my annual review, officially making it a series. As always, what follows are some surprising, entertaining, or enlightening things I stumbled upon in 2023.

  1. South Korea has a unique way of counting a person’s age 🇰🇷👴. South Korea has enacted a new law that modifies the method for calculating ages, transitioning from the traditional “Korean age” system to the international standard. Currently, South Korea employs three age-counting systems, yet the majority of citizens follow the “Korean age,” wherein a person is considered 1 year old at birth and gains an additional year on every New Year’s Day. Consequently, a baby born on Dec. 31 would be regarded as 2 years old the following day.

item.title: Books I Read in 2022
item.description: I’m glad I got into reading more books again in 2022. The internet and YouTube, in particular, have such a strong pull that I almost have to force myself to take time and dedicate myself to reading something longer than an article. Also, I’m a terribly slow reader, which is just unbearable when I see people casually reading twice as fast as me. Still, I found great satisfaction in committing and extending my attention span beyond the instant rewards of today’s internet.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2021
item.description:
Introduction

Welcome to “Things I Learned in 2021”! For the second year now, here are noteworthy things that stood out to me during last year.

  1. Hippocampal replay is a phenomenon observed in animals where sequences of cell activations in the hippocampus, a brain region associated with memory and spatial navigation, re-occur during sleep or awake rest at a much faster time scale 🧠🐈🐀⏰. Hippocampal replay is a phenomenon observed in animals where sequences of cell activations in the hippocampus, a brain region associated with memory and spatial navigation, re-occur during sleep at a much faster time scale than during the original activity. This behavior is exhibited by place cells, which fire in a sequence according to the animal’s movement path. The phenomenon has been observed in various animals and linked to memory consolidation. Studies have also found instances of preplay, where a sequence of activations occurs before the actual activity and replays in reverse.

item.title: Things I Learned in 2020
item.description:
In this blog post, I’ll share some of the interesting and unexpected things I came across on the internet in 2020. Without further ado, here are the 25 things that stood out to me.

  1. Brown is not a color, and there is no brown light 🟤🙅‍♂️🎨.

  2. The temperature and atmospheric pressure on Earth can vary greatly across its surface. However, there are lines around the Earth called Isothermal lines and Isobar lines where the temperature and pressure are the same. These lines are jagged in shape, and they intersect at two points, creating at least two points on Earth that have the exact same temperature and pressure at any given time 🌍.
